takeUp.intent: The heartbeat of a node. For now it is an X-minute loop (start with 10) that fires an action list which is empty until we fill it, and it must be able to 'Tell Mom' - the notify/report protocol for when a cycle has something to say. It grows by adding actions, not by changing the beat. Its own module and door, displayed in the Menu beside Echidna; the cycle number the LAN rows show comes from it, not from Core.

takeUp.title: Phoenix Cycle: a registration registry like Event_Handler and the Process Manager
takeUp.intent: Phoenix is not a scheduler that knows what maintenance is - it is a registry that runs entries raised by their owners, exactly as Event_Handler and the Process Manager work. Every entry carries BOTH surfaces: an in-process tick thread the owner implements and an HTTP port the owner answers, because a thread-only entry is an invisible background process (forbidden) and a port-only entry needs a caller to remember it (the thing this module exists to remove). Triggers are declared - every / cron / on(event) / after(DAG refs) - never inferred. Every run leaves a receipt, every action runs under a lease so one slow entry cannot starve the rest, and the whole cycle plus its children stops on one close button. An empty registry is correct on a fresh install. Spec written at docs/spec/phoenix-registry.md. Done means: registry.json is honoured, six seed code entries plus two nag entries run and leave receipts, a nag surfaces one at a time in the monitor with TL;DR buttons, and stopping the cycle cancels outstanding leases honestly.
next: module/Phoenix scaffolding: registry.json, thread tick, port with GET /api/entries and POST /api/tick

takeUp.title: Every node runs Hermes and a llama.cpp model sized to its card, as a service
takeUp.intent: Hydra is Hermes-happy: for a node to be part of the fleet it offers two things - a Hermes agent (so the node can be given a job, not just a port) and a llama.cpp server with a model that actually fits its VRAM. That pair is what makes local housekeeping possible at all: the caretaker job never leaves the LAN and never touches a paid provider. Done means every live node advertises {hermes, llama} in its state caps, the model choice is derived from measured VRAM (not from the card's marketing name), the Process Manager supervises llama-server through WATCHDOG_TABLE so it is visible and stoppable, and the caretaker role can be filed on any node that advertises both.

takeUp.title: Agents reach Hydra through MCP, not through a prose brief
takeUp.intent: The mother brief is a crutch: it teaches Echidna by lecture. Any agent - including a 2B local model - should instead be handed tools and discover the fleet by calling them, so a tiny model needs no briefing and no long context. Hydra's MCP door already exists and answers at http://127.0.0.1:8126/mcp (protocol 2025-06-18, serverInfo event-handler, tools event_list/event_trigger/event_log/event_purge verified by a live initialize + tools/list). Two steps remain: (1) register that endpoint with Hermes so every spawned agent inherits it as an MCP server, including the Echidna chat instance and any 'hermes -z' caretaker; (2) add Easy-button tools to the Hydra MCP with zero required arguments - hydra_monitor (the top card), hydra_tot (bullets), hydra_phoenix (upkeep), hydra_doors (what is up) - so a small model can orient in one call each. The prose brief then shrinks to identity only, and remains as the fallback when the MCP door is down.

takeUp.title: MAME machines: the eight old laptops become arcade cabinets
takeUp.intent: Operator idea (2026-11-07): turn roughly eight spare old laptops into dedicated arcade machines - Linux Mint + MAME + operator-supplied ROMs. The design constraint is that from the player seat Linux does not exist: power on, and a game is running. The front end must be a full-screen cabinet-style ROM selector that remembers the last game and boots straight into it unless the player deliberately re-selects, with keyboard/joystick only, no mouse, no desktop, no window border, no cursor. Success is measured in boot-to-gameplay seconds on the slowest laptop that still runs at full frame rate.
next: pick the front end against old-laptop limits: Attract Mode (lightest, themes are just Squirrel), EmulationStation (heavier, GL), Pegasus (Qt, prettier but heavier), versus a purpose-built kiosk launcher - note that "boot the last game" is NOT a stock feature of any of them, so it is either a theme script or a wrapper

define the kiosk session: autologin, X with no desktop and no window manager, frontend as the only client, cursor hidden, and a systemd user unit that starts it - so the laptop never shows a login, a panel or a wallpaper

build ONE golden image and clone it eight times: unattended Mint install plus a postinstall that drops MAME, the front end, the ROM set, per-machine config and the autostart, instead of hand-building each laptop

decide the input: USB gamepad per laptop (cheapest, instantly mappable) versus a keyboard encoder and real arcade buttons; MAME wants 6 buttons plus a stick per player, and some laptop keyboards ghost beyond 3 simultaneous keys
decide where ROMs live (per-laptop disk, or one SD card per machine) and pin the MAME version to the ROM set - a mismatched set silently boots to a black screen on half the titles

measure the honest ceiling per laptop: MAME is CPU-bound, so 1980s-90s 2D titles (CPS1/2, Neo Geo) are fine while 3D-era games will not hold frame rate no matter the settings; record boot-to-game seconds and frames per second per machine
